statement: Whole numbers a, b and c are such that a + b is odd and b + c is odd. Which of these must be odd?

choices.misconception: I thought that because a + b and b + c are both odd, a + c must be odd as well.
I assumed b had to be the odd number in each sum, forgetting that a and c could be the odd ones with b even.
I tested a = 1, b = 2, c = 3, got a × c = 3, and assumed one example proved it always works.
I tested a = 2, b = 1, c = 4, got a + b + c = 7, and took that single example as proof.

hints: Compare whether a is odd or even with whether c is.
An odd sum needs one odd number and one even number. So a and b have different parity, and so do b and c. Decide what that says about a and c together.
Both a and c differ in parity from b, so a and c have the same parity, which makes a + c even.

solutions.reliable: An odd sum needs one odd and one even number, so a and b have different parity, and b and c have different parity. Then a and c have the same parity, so a + c is even and a + c + 1 is always odd. The others can fail: a = 1, b = 2, c = 3 makes b and a + b + c even, and a = 2, b = 1, c = 4 makes a × c and a + c even. The transferable idea: track odd and even rather than values; a 'must' needs a reason, and one counterexample rules it out.
solutions.elegant: (a + b) + (b + c) = a + c + 2b is odd plus odd, which is even. Taking away the even number 2b leaves a + c even, so a + c + 1 is odd.

whyOnTest: Parity questions reward tracking odd and even instead of values, and a single counterexample rules out each choice that is only sometimes odd.
